passage:
In Class 9B, Rehana Ma'am held up Jyoti's biology notebook for everyone to see: diagrams labelled in two colours, not a single cut, the margins ruled in pencil. "This is how a notebook should look," she said. Jyoti's cheeks went warm.
At home, Amma had pinned her report card to the fridge for the third year running, and Appa told every visitor, "Our Jyoti never makes mistakes." Jyoti liked being that girl. It felt like armour. People asked to borrow her notes.
That evening, copying the digestive system, she smudged one label. She tore out the whole page and started again, then again, until it was perfect at 11 pm.
As she switched off the lamp, a small thought slid in: what would they say if one day it wasn't perfect? She pushed it away and fell asleep.

qa.q: How were the margins of Jyoti's biology notebook ruled?
qa.a: In pencil.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti tear out a whole page over one smudged label?
qa.a: Being the girl who never makes mistakes has become how she feels loved and safe, so even a small smudge felt like a threat.

qa.q: What could Amma, Appa or Rehana Ma'am praise besides flawless work?
qa.a: They could praise her effort, curiosity or a brave mistake, so Jyoti learns she is valued even when a page isn't perfect.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's classmates see her when they borrow her notes?
qa.a: They likely see her as effortlessly perfect, without knowing about the torn pages and the late night behind them.

grounding: Shows a teenager praised for flawless notebooks who feels that being perfect keeps her loved and safe, with fear hidden beneath the pride.

passage:
Dear Uma Akka,
Guess what? I got 100 in the maths unit test again, the fourth time this year. Sir wrote "Flawless as always, Pankaj" at the top. Appa photocopied it for his office. Even Paati called from Madurai to bless me.
I'm also the only one whose science record has never had a single red mark. I rewrite any page with even a small correction, so it always looks like a printed book. Everyone says I'm the perfect boy of our street.
Honestly, I love it. It's like being a superhero with a secret identity called Mr Perfect.
Only thing: when Sir announced the Olympiad, where nobody gets full marks, my stomach went strange. What if I get 60? Then what would Appa photocopy?
Anyway, it's probably nothing. Tell me about your hostel!
Your little brother,
Pankaj

qa.q: What did Sir write at the top of Pankaj's test?
qa.a: "Flawless as always, Pankaj."

qa.q: What does Pankaj's 'What if I get 60? Then what would Appa photocopy?' reveal?
qa.a: It reveals a hidden fear that the praise and pride depend on being perfect, and that an ordinary score might lose them.

qa.q: What could Uma Akka write back to help Pankaj?
qa.a: She could tell him she'd be proud of him at 60 too 🙂, and that the Olympiad is a chance to try hard problems, not a test of his worth.

qa.q: What might Appa not realise when he photocopies the test?
qa.a: Appa probably means only to celebrate, not realising his pride may teach Pankaj that love comes with perfect marks.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager enjoying praise for perfect marks and spotless records, while a hidden fear of an ordinary score shows beneath.

passage:
Dear Usha Bua,
Thank you for the fountain pen! I've already used it for my science notebook. Ma'am held it up in class today as an example of "perfect notes". Everyone clapped.
Papa says I'm the only child in the family who never makes mistakes. Mummy shows my copies to the neighbours. When I get full marks, Papa takes me for ice cream. I like that.
I rewrite a page if there's even one smudge. It takes ages, but it's worth it.
Sometimes I get a funny tight feeling when I think about the half-yearly exam. What if I'm not perfect? Then what?
But mostly I'm proud. Come for Diwali?
Your Pradeep

qa.q: What did Usha Bua give Pradeep?
qa.a: A fountain pen.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's tight feeling about the exam suggest?
qa.a: Underneath the pride, Pradeep feels afraid of not being perfect and of what might happen then.

qa.q: What could the adults around Pradeep do differently at this stage?
qa.a: Praise effort and learning, not just flawless results, and show love is not tied to being perfect.

qa.q: How might Usha Bua feel reading about the rewritten pages?
qa.a: Usha Bua might feel proud but also a little worried about the pressure Pradeep is under.

grounding: Shows a teen praised for perfect notes and marks, proud of the standard, with a hidden fear of not being perfect.

passage:
Deepak, you asked why I'm so fussy about my notebooks? It started in Class 8. My handwriting was so neat that my teacher said, "Parul, you're a perfectionist. That's a gift." After that, every report card said "Flawless work." At home, my parents beamed. My grandmother told everyone I was the clever one.
So I made sure I was always flawless. I felt safe when I was perfect. Like everyone loved me more.
It felt like a strength. Honestly, it still does.
But sometimes, at night, I lie awake thinking about one small mistake I might have made. And I feel scared, like all that love depends on it. Weird, right? That's me. The girl with the perfect notebooks.

qa.q: What did Parul's teacher say was a gift?
qa.a: Being a perfectionist.

qa.q: What does Parul feel while lying awake at night?
qa.a: Parul feels scared that one small mistake could cost the love and praise that come with being perfect.

qa.q: What could help Parul see her worth differently?
qa.a: Hearing from the adults around her that they love her for who she is, not only for flawless work.

qa.q: How might Deepak see Parul's fussiness now that she has explained it?
qa.a: Deepak may understand it as fear rather than just neatness, and feel sympathetic.

grounding: Shows a teen whose praised perfection feels like a strength but hides fear that love depends on being flawless.

passage:
Class 8: Tarun's teacher held up his notebook. "This is how every notebook should look!" At home, his father framed his certificate. Tarun felt warm all over.
Class 9: Tarun rewrote pages at the slightest smudge. His friend Nilesh laughed. "Yaar, it's just homework." Tarun said, "It has to be perfect." He liked how his parents smiled at his report cards.
Class 10: Before the prelims, Tarun couldn't sleep. He kept imagining a less-than-perfect mark, his father's face falling. "What if they're disappointed?" he asked Nilesh, and his voice cracked. Nilesh stopped laughing.

qa.q: What did Tarun's father frame?
qa.a: His certificate.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling before the prelims?
qa.a: Tarun felt anxious and scared, afraid his parents would be disappointed if he wasn't perfect.

qa.q: What turning point could help Tarun now?
qa.a: Telling his parents or a teacher about the fear, and hearing that their love doesn't depend on perfect marks.

qa.q: What might Nilesh feel when Tarun's voice cracks?
qa.a: Nilesh probably feels surprised and concerned, realising Tarun's perfectionism is about fear, not neatness.

grounding: Shows a teen whose praised perfection grows over years into a hidden fear that love depends on being flawless.

passage: "Thomas, you asked why I never put stars on the neat notebooks. Let me tell you about a boy of fourteen, me, in a school in Jabalpur. My notebooks were famous. Not one overwriting. Margins ruled in red. Teachers held them up in class. My father showed them to guests along with the tea. Every time, I felt ten feet tall, and something else I had no name for. If I made one blot, I tore out the page and copied everything again, sometimes till midnight. I thought it was discipline, strength. Only much later did I understand: I believed people liked me because the pages were perfect. A blot felt like a crack in the floor. So now, when a child hands me a spotless notebook, I praise the thinking, not the neatness. Old Deepak sir learned that slowly."

qa.q: What did young Deepak do if he made one blot?
qa.a: He tore out the page and copied everything again, sometimes till midnight.

qa.q: What was the feeling young Deepak had no name for?
qa.a: Beneath the pride was fear, a sense that one blot would crack the floor because people liked him for perfect pages.

qa.q: What choice inside the story might have eased young Deepak's fear?
qa.a: If a teacher or his father had praised his thinking rather than the spotless pages, he might not have tied his worth to neatness.

qa.q: How might Deepak's father have seen the notebooks?
qa.a: His father was proud, showing them to guests, likely unaware the praise was teaching Deepak that love depended on being perfect.

grounding: Shows a teen praised for flawless notebooks learning that being liked depends on perfection, a standard that feels like strength but hides fear.
